strengths: The paper studies an important problem—small-data offline black-box optimization—and proposes a coherent adaptation of an 8B diffusion language model using domain adaptation, supervised fine-tuning, and reward-weighted post-training.

The empirical headline is promising: over eight seeds and 128 proposals per task, DiBO obtains the best aggregate mean and median ranks across four Design-Bench tasks, with especially large best-candidate gains on TF Bind 8 and Ant Morphology. Reporting both 100th- and 50th-percentile performance is more informative than reporting only the best candidate.

The experiments include diverse baseline families and useful ablations. The delimiter, training-stage, and similarity-conditioned-context studies show consistent component-level effects, while the sensitivity studies cover context length, dataset size, RL learning rate, and prompt wording.

The unified text representation supports discrete sequences and continuous morphology vectors without task-specific output architectures. This is a useful and moderately original application of diffusion LLMs, although the individual ingredients are largely established.

The manuscript is generally organized and readable, and the rendered figures and tables are legible. It reports the base model, optimizer, precision, principal learning rates, batch accumulation, hardware, candidate budget, seed count, and approximate runtime.

The impact statement appropriately identifies dataset bias and dual-use risks in biochemical design, emphasizes expert oversight, and does not raise an unresolved ethical barrier. weaknesses: The central RL formulation is not technically convincing as written. Equation 6 introduces an approximation to log p(o|q), but Equation 7 optimizes token probabilities pθ rather than log probabilities. This is neither the stated policy-gradient objective nor a standard likelihood objective, and its gradient behavior differs materially. Moreover, assuming an unknown behavior policy is uniform does not by itself justify omitting importance correction, clipping, or KL regularization in offline RL. A derivation and corrected algorithm are necessary.

The domain-adaptation objective in Equation 3 is internally inconsistent: the indicator selects masked response tokens oi, while the text claims joint reconstruction of prompt and response, and the indexed term pθ(qi,oi|qt,ot) is ill-defined when prompt and response lengths differ. This ambiguity affects a central claimed stage rather than a peripheral detail.

The evidence does not isolate the proposed explanation that bidirectional diffusion modeling is responsible for the gains. OPRO uses a different pretrained model and training regime, while the closest inference-only diffusion-LLM baseline is excluded from the main table. A controlled autoregressive 8B model trained on the same corpus with comparable DA/SFT/reward training is needed to separate architecture from data construction, compute, and post-training.

Evaluation is limited to four Design-Bench tasks, and full component ablations appear on only TF Bind 8 and Ant. Several claims—such as robustness, generality, and the necessity of every stage—are therefore broader than the evidence. Statistical significance tests or paired confidence intervals are also absent despite overlapping standard deviations in some comparisons.

The offline-data protocol is insufficiently specified and potentially consequential. The paper says it evenly subsamples a label-sorted dataset and then assigns the lower 80% to prompts and upper 20% to targets, but does not give exact indexing, pair counts, reuse frequencies, or source splits. The reported D(best) values are difficult to reconcile with an endpoint-preserving even subsample of the full label-sorted data. Exact construction code and a leakage audit are needed.

Baseline comparability cannot be verified. Although the paper states that all methods use the same 500-point pool, it does not document baseline implementations, tuning budgets, checkpoints, or per-method hyperparameter searches. DiBO receives an 8B pretrained model, multiple training stages, and prompt-template generation, so equal data alone does not ensure a fair comparison.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for an 8B-model pipeline: the manuscript omits the numbers of optimization steps or epochs per stage, numbers of DA/SFT/RL examples, mask and decoding schedules, response parsing and invalid-output handling, continuous-variable clipping, checkpoint selection, and complete seed-dependent construction. The abstract says code is available “here,” but the manuscript does not provide a visible repository identifier or archival snapshot.

Similarity-conditioned prompt construction is responsible for a very large TF Bind 8 gain, suggesting that data pairing may be at least as important as the diffusion architecture. Yet it is not compared against stronger retrieval or nearest-neighbor optimization baselines, and it is unclear whether all learned baselines receive an equivalent locality mechanism.

The evaluation relies on benchmark oracles and normalized scores using extrema from an unobserved full dataset. This is conventional for Design-Bench evaluation, but the paper should discuss oracle validity, duplicate/generated training designs, novelty and feasibility rates, and whether continuous candidates remain within valid parameter bounds.

The technical limitations discussion is thin. The paper acknowledges societal risks but does not adequately discuss benchmark-oracle error, substantial H100/8B-model cost, dependence on serialized three-decimal continuous values, limited task coverage, or the gap between simulated oracle scores and physical scientific validation. Overall, the promising results merit further work, but the objective inconsistencies and missing controlled/reproducible evidence prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly motivated and organized, with a readable overview of the proposed domain-adaptation, supervised fine-tuning, and reward-based training pipeline. Empirically, DiBO obtains strong best-of-128 results on three of four Design-Bench tasks, with particularly large reported gains on TF Bind 8 and Ant Morphology. Results are averaged over eight seeds, and median-candidate results supplement the optimistic maximum-score metric.

The ablations examine delimiter tokens, individual training stages, similarity-conditioned context construction, prompt wording, dataset size, context length, and RL learning rate. These experiments indicate that the complete recipe works better than several simplified variants.
The method is computationally feasible relative to its 8B-parameter backbone: the authors report single-H100 training and roughly 1.5 hours for the TF Bind 8 pipeline.

The impact statement appropriately acknowledges dataset bias, expert-oversight requirements, and potential misuse in biochemical design. Given the benchmark-only experiments, there is no clear unresolved ethical issue requiring rejection.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central explanation—that bidirectional diffusion modeling is responsible for the gains—is not tested. There is no parameter- and training-matched autoregressive model using the same corpus, delimiters, SFT data, reward objective, and compute. OPRO is an inference-style LLaMA baseline, so the experiments cannot distinguish diffusion architecture from extensive task-specific training, data construction, or model choice.

Soundness: the evaluation-time prompt construction is not specified. Training contexts are selected by similarity to the known target response, but at deployment that response is precisely the unknown quantity. The paper does not explain how the prompts producing the 128 evaluation candidates are selected, whether training prompts are reused, or how target-conditioned context construction is implemented without privileged information. This is a potentially decisive validity and leakage concern.

Soundness: the purported RL stage is technically unclear. Equation 6 introduces a sum of log probabilities, whereas Equation 7 optimizes token probabilities rather than log probabilities. The data consist of fixed offline prompt-response pairs with ground-truth rewards, making the procedure closer to signed reward-weighted behavior cloning than a justified policy-gradient method. Assuming an unknown old policy is uniform does not by itself justify dropping clipping and KL regularization, and negative uncentered rewards can create poorly characterized behavior.

Soundness: Equation 3 is internally inconsistent with the claimed joint prompt-response reconstruction: its mask indicator indexes only response tokens while the logarithm jointly references prompt and response tokens. These mathematical ambiguities prevent verification of what was actually optimized.

Evaluation breadth is limited to four Design-Bench tasks, with ablations only on two. The primary metric is the maximum oracle score among 128 samples, which is highly sensitive to tail behavior. Median results help, but DiBO is weak on D’Kitty median performance relative to numerous baselines. No diversity, validity rate, distance from training designs, exact-match rate, or out-of-distribution analysis is provided, so memorization of high-ranked response targets is not ruled out.

The offline pool is constructed by sorting the complete benchmark by label and evenly subsampling across that ordering. This assumes access to a deliberately label-stratified pool spanning the full score range and weakens the claimed realism of scarce, naturally collected offline data. The 80/20 lower-versus-higher partition then supplies the model with explicitly selected high-score targets. Robustness to random, biased, or low-quality offline collections is not studied.

Originality is modest and insufficiently isolated. Delimiter tokens, masked-model domain adaptation, SFT, and offline reward weighting are individually standard ingredients. Applying their combination to a diffusion LLM for BBO is potentially useful, but the paper does not establish a new diffusion-specific insight or demonstrate that an autoregressive model cannot benefit equally from the same recipe.

Baseline treatment is incomplete. The text initially lists the most directly related frozen diffusion-LLM-plus-MCTS method as a baseline, but it is omitted from the quantitative table because it uses a different data regime. No adapted comparison is supplied, and training budgets, tuning procedures, and implementation details for the remaining baselines are largely absent, making fairness difficult to assess.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the claimed code link. Essential details are missing, including the number and construction multiplicity of prompt-response pairs, optimization steps or stopping criteria for every stage, checkpoint selection, inference prompts, denoising steps and schedule, temperature or sampling controls, invalid-output handling, and exact baseline configurations. The phrase “Code ... is available here” also does not expose a usable repository location in the reviewed manuscript.

Presentation is visually polished, but several claims overreach the evidence: “robust and general,” applicability across diverse domains, and explanations based on bidirectional dependencies are asserted without the necessary controlled comparisons. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations section discussing target-conditioned context construction, label-stratified sampling, 8B-model cost, benchmark-oracle dependence, or the narrow task set. Overall, the strong headline scores are not enough to overcome the unresolved protocol and objective ambiguities.

strengths: The paper introduces a coherent framework combining diffusion-LLM domain adaptation, response-only supervised fine-tuning, and reward-based post-training. The reported empirical performance is promising: over eight seeds, DiBO has the best aggregate mean and median rank for the 100th-percentile metric and leads on three of four tasks, including a sizable TF Bind 8 margin.

The evaluation covers discrete biological sequences and high-dimensional continuous morphology vectors, and includes 50th-percentile results rather than relying exclusively on best-of-128 performance.

Ablations provide evidence that delimiters, all three training stages, and similarity-based prompt construction contribute to performance. Sensitivity analyses also examine context size, offline-pool size, RL learning rate, and prompt wording.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. It provides a relevant impact statement that acknowledges dataset bias, dual-use biological risks, and the need for expert oversight.
weaknesses: The central explanation—that bidirectional diffusion modeling is responsible for the gains—is not experimentally isolated. OPRO is an inference-time autoregressive baseline, whereas DiBO receives extensive task-specific DA, SFT, and RL. A matched autoregressive model trained with the same data construction, objectives, parameter scale, and compute is essential; without it, the results support the complete pipeline but not the claimed advantage of diffusion or bidirectionality.

The mathematical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Equation 3 is described as joint prompt-response reconstruction but its mask indicator and summation refer only to response tokens, while the probability term jointly indexes prompt and response tokens. Equation 6 defines an approximate log probability, but Equation 7 unexpectedly optimizes raw token probabilities rather than log probabilities. This is not the standard reward-weighted/policy-gradient objective, and the discussion of a uniform old policy, clipping, and KL regularization does not derive the displayed loss.

The inference protocol is under-specified. The paper does not clearly state how evaluation prompts are constructed, how many prompts produce the 128 candidates, the denoising-step schedule, sampling temperature or selection procedure, handling of invalid outputs, or whether candidates duplicating any of the 500 offline designs are rejected. Because high-scoring offline designs are directly used as supervised response targets, novelty and nearest-neighbor/duplicate statistics are important for ruling out replay or local memorization.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate despite the stated code link. The manuscript omits the number of optimization steps or epochs per stage, the number of constructed prompt-response and RL pairs, model checkpointing and selection rules, detailed baseline configurations and tuning budgets, and exact numerical sensitivity results. Referring to the base model's official defaults does not fully specify the training and decoding pipeline.

The evidence is narrower than the broad general-purpose claims suggest: only four Design-Bench tasks are evaluated, all component ablations are restricted to TF Bind 8 and Ant, and no statistical tests or paired-seed comparisons are reported. The 50th-percentile table is also mixed—DiBO trails another method on TF Bind 8 and several methods on D’Kitty—so claims of uniformly strong candidate quality should be qualified.

The comparison to the closest diffusion-LLM work is deferred rather than measured because it targets a different pool size. Evaluating that method at its intended regime, and evaluating DiBO under the same regime, would better establish originality and the practical value of post-training.

Overall, the idea and results are promising, but the missing controlled autoregressive comparison, ambiguous objectives, and incomplete inference/reproducibility details prevent reliable validation of the main claims in the current version. These issues outweigh the empirical merits, although they appear addressable in a substantial revision.

strengths: The paper explores a timely and potentially useful direction: adapting pretrained diffusion language models to small-data offline black-box optimization across both sequence and continuous design spaces.

The empirical study is broad in several respects: four main Design-Bench tasks, eight random seeds, numerous classical and generative baselines, maximum and median/Top-K metrics, three additional RNA tasks, and ablations of training stages, delimiters, context selection, sampling, and hyperparameters.

The reported main-benchmark results are strong. DiBO has the best aggregate rank and improves substantially on Ant Morphology and TF Bind 8; the matched autoregressive comparison and stage ablations are useful attempts to investigate the source of these gains.

Presentation is generally clear, with a helpful overview figure, concrete prompt examples, training schedules, sample counts, hardware/runtime information, and a behavioral audit for possible benchmark knowledge in the pretrained model. The impact statement appropriately acknowledges dataset bias and dual-use risks in biological design.
weaknesses: The central bidirectional-generation explanation is not adequately supported. At inference, the paper fills a fully masked response greedily in a single forward pass rather than iteratively denoising it. Consequently, response positions do not observe generated prefix or suffix tokens, making it unclear how the claimed bidirectional dependencies among design variables are represented during generation. No dependency-controlled synthetic experiment or comparison against iterative diffusion decoding is provided.

The purportedly matched diffusion-versus-autoregressive experiment does not isolate architecture: LLADA-8B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct differ in pretraining data, objectives, tokenizers, and instruction tuning. Moreover, an autoregressive model cannot literally retain the same likelihood factorization and training/inference pipeline. The continuous-task gains at the final stage are only 0.011 and 0.001, without statistical tests. Thus Table 2 does not establish that bidirectionality causes the improvements.

The RL formulation is technically questionable and insufficiently justified. Equation 6 introduces an approximate log probability, but Equation 7 optimizes reward-weighted token probabilities rather than log probabilities. Assuming an unknown behavior policy is uniform does not by itself justify dropping importance ratios, clipping, and KL control; the resulting update is not a standard policy-gradient or offline-RL objective and may drive probabilities toward degenerate boundaries. There is no comparison with reward-weighted supervised learning or another offline preference objective to show that the claimed RL mechanism is necessary.

Dataset construction is internally unclear. Appendix A.2 describes D1 as lower-scoring prompt designs and D2 as higher-scoring response targets, which would make response improvements positive, yet the RL dataset is claimed to contain approximately balanced positive and negative rewards. The exact RL pairing procedure, corpus sizes, reuse frequency, and distinction among DA, SFT, and RL examples are not specified well enough to resolve this contradiction or reproduce training.

The evaluation does not establish that generated candidates are novel relative to the complete 500-point offline pool or the repeatedly used response targets; candidates are only required to differ from examples in the current prompt. This is important because an 8B model is trained for thousands of updates on a very small pool. Nearest-neighbor distances, exact training-set match rates, and results excluding memorized outputs are needed. Continuing generation until 128 unique valid outputs also leaves the attempted-sample/compute budget unspecified and potentially unequal to baselines.

The generality and robustness claims are overstated. There are only four main tasks, while on all three added RNA tasks DiBO is worse than the compared baselines on most Top-5/10/20 and median metrics; it wins only the maximum on two tasks. The closest prior inference-only diffusion-LLM method is discussed but omitted from all quantitative comparisons, and baseline tuning/configuration details are incomplete.

Reproducibility is only partial: several prompt vectors are abbreviated, complete templates and validity/range handling for continuous outputs are absent, baseline hyperparameters and compute budgets are not fully reported, and the displayed code link is not concretely identified in the manuscript text. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations discussion covering the narrow benchmark set, dependence on benchmark oracles, memorization risk, large-model compute, and the weak RNA candidate-set results. The ethics statement is appropriate but generic and gives no concrete safeguards for biological deployment.

strengths: [Originality/significance] Adapting a pretrained diffusion language model to offline black-box optimization through a unified prompt/design/label representation is a potentially useful direction. The delimiter-based interface is simple and applicable to heterogeneous design spaces.

[Empirical evidence] On the four main Design-Bench tasks, DiBO has the best aggregate rank over eight seeds and improves substantially on TF Bind 8; the paper also reports median and Top-K results rather than only best-of-128 performance.

[Experimental analysis] The training-stage, delimiter, context-selection, data-size, prompt-template, and learning-rate studies are useful. The matched 8B autoregressive comparison is more informative than comparing only against small task-specific models.

[Limitations/ethics] The pretraining-overlap probe is a welcome attempt to address contamination, and the impact statement acknowledges dataset bias and biochemical dual-use risks without overstating the audit's conclusiveness.
weaknesses: [Soundness—decisive] The purported RL objective is not adequately justified and appears inconsistent with the preceding derivation. Equation 6 introduces a sum of token log-probabilities, but Equation 7 optimizes the average of token probabilities multiplied by reward. This is neither the stated sequence log-likelihood objective nor a valid sequence-level importance-sampling estimator: replacing an unavailable behavior policy by a uniform constant does not justify replacing the sequence probability/product with a sum of marginal token probabilities. No theorem, derivation, or comparison with standard reward-weighted log-likelihood is provided. This weakens a central methodological contribution.

[Evaluation validity—decisive] The model is trained on high-label response targets from D2 and then evaluated on generations for the same task, but the manuscript only says that duplicate generated outputs are removed. It does not state that candidates matching any of the 500 offline designs—especially memorized high-label D2 targets—are excluded. Because the main metric is the best of 128 and the model repeatedly sees these targets during DA/SFT/RL, the evaluation needs an explicit whole-pool novelty check and separate reporting for genuinely novel candidates. D(best) being below the best DiBO result does not rule out inflation of median or Top-K results through memorization.

[Claim attribution] The LLaDA-versus-LLaMA comparison does not isolate bidirectionality. The backbones have different pretraining corpora, objectives, tokenizers, and instruction-tuning histories, while only downstream data and training stages are matched. Thus the results establish that this particular LLaDA checkpoint performs better, not that bidirectional modeling causes the gain. No controlled architectural experiment or dependency-specific diagnostic supports the paper's central explanation.

[Missing closest comparison] The related-work section identifies a contemporaneous inference-only diffusion-LLM optimizer, and the baseline section even lists it as dLLM, but it is absent from Table 1. The explanation that it originally targets n_pool=10 is not a reason to omit a re-evaluation under the paper's n_pool=500 protocol. This leaves the incremental value of expensive task-specific post-training over the closest diffusion-LLM alternative unclear.

[Significance/generalization] The main evidence covers only four benchmarks, including very small length-8 and length-10 DNA spaces. The additional RNA results are substantially mixed: DiBO loses all reported metrics on RNA-B and often has worse Top-5/10/20 and median performance on RNA-A/C despite occasionally winning the maximum. Consequently, claims of robust, consistent, general-purpose optimization across scientific domains are stronger than the evidence supports.

[Baseline fairness and efficiency] DiBO fine-tunes an 8B model separately for every task on an H100, but training cost, tuning effort, and compute-matched comparisons are not reported for most baselines. Equalizing only the 128 oracle-evaluation candidates does not establish equal overall computational budgets. The practical value relative to much smaller offline optimizers is therefore unclear.

[Reproducibility] Although the abstract says code is available “here,” the supplied manuscript contains no resolvable code URL. Full prompt templates, baseline hyperparameters, construction counts for DA/SFT/RL pairs, checkpoint details, random seeds, and exact validity/novelty filters are also missing. The reported results would be difficult to independently reproduce from the paper alone.

[Presentation/limitations] Several mathematical definitions are ambiguous—for example, Equation 3 uses a joint masking indicator and a joint token probability while prompt and response have different roles and potentially different lengths. The paper also lacks a dedicated limitations discussion covering memorization, dependence on pretrained-model provenance, large per-task compute, weak RNA set quality, or the heuristic nature of the RL loss.

[Ethics] The dual-use discussion is appropriate but generic. For biochemical deployment, the paper proposes no concrete access control, screening, validation, or uncertainty protocol; this is not independently disqualifying for benchmark-only work, but it limits the claimed readiness for sensitive scientific use.

strengths: The paper presents a useful and reasonably original combination of diffusion-language-model adaptation, structured delimiter tokens, supervised fine-tuning, and reward-based post-training for offline black-box optimization. Applying an instruction-tuned diffusion LLM to heterogeneous design, label, and text inputs is a meaningful contribution.

The main empirical results are strong: DiBO has the best aggregate mean score (0.897) and median rank (1.0), and obtains the best maximum score on three of four Design-Bench tasks, including a sizable improvement on TF Bind 8.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this setting. It includes forward, inverse, autoregressive, diffusion, evolutionary, and MCTS baselines; eight random seeds; maximum, median, and Top-K metrics; additional RNA tasks; and stronger dimension-scaled GP baselines.

The ablations are informative. Delimiter tokens, all three training stages, and similarity-conditioned contexts each improve performance. The matched 8B diffusion-versus-autoregressive comparison is particularly valuable, with the largest diffusion gains appearing on the discrete sequence tasks targeted by the motivation.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The manuscript provides learning rates, step counts, batch accumulation, hardware, pool size, context size, decoding details, and prompt examples, while the impact statement appropriately acknowledges dataset bias, dual-use biological-design risks, and the need for expert oversight.

The pretraining-overlap ranking probe is a thoughtful attempt to address possible benchmark contamination; performance close to random ranking provides some evidence against the pretrained model already knowing the task-specific design-label relationships.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully establish the paper's central causal claim that bidirectional modeling is responsible for the gains. LLaDA-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B differ in pretraining, tokenization, and instruction tuning in addition to generation architecture, and the manuscript does not explain precisely how the masked DA/SFT objectives were translated to the autoregressive model. Thus Table 2 is matched at the downstream-pipeline level but not a clean architectural control.

The reinforcement-learning formulation needs stronger justification. Equation 7 optimizes token probabilities rather than the log-probability approximation introduced in Equation 6, treats an unknown behavior policy as uniform, omits importance-ratio clipping and KL control, and applies offline sequence rewards through independently scored tokens. This resembles reward-weighted offline fitting, and no analysis demonstrates that the approximation is reliable or preferable to simpler weighted SFT.

The claimed generality is broader than the evidence. The main suite contains only four tasks, including very short DNA sequences of lengths 8 and 10. On the three additional RNA tasks, DiBO wins the best-of-128 metric only on RNA-A and RNA-C but is often substantially worse on Top-5/10/20 and median quality, and it loses all reported metrics on RNA-B. These results suggest strength in finding occasional maxima rather than consistently generating high-quality designs.

The main metric is the maximum among 128 candidates and can be sensitive to tail behavior. The appendix's Top-K and median results help, but DiBO is not consistently superior on D'Kitty or the RNA tasks, so the state-of-the-art and robustness language should be narrowed.

Important reproducibility details remain underspecified: only representative rather than all ten prompt templates are given, continuous-vector examples are abbreviated, the exact construction of similarity-conditioned contexts at inference is unclear, and invalid-output handling has no maximum retry or compute budget. The PDF's statement that code is available 'here' does not contain a functioning link in the submitted file.

Evaluation relies entirely on benchmark oracles, with no assessment of oracle reliability for generated out-of-distribution designs or any real experimental validation. This is standard for Design-Bench but materially limits the scientific-discovery claims. Overall, the work is promising and acceptance-worthy, but these soundness and scope limitations favor a weak accept rather than a full accept.
